designIntent: Publication-quality board narrative inspired by strong research publications: argument-led sequence, purpose-built visual relationships, commentary that synthesises rather than repeats, and silent editorial restraint.

slides.communicationGoal: Establish the single category-level proposition before exposing detail.
slides.headlineIntent: The category is becoming more competitive — but the pressure is coming from three different directions.
slides.content: Minimal cover: Pulse acquisition momentum; Northstar customer vulnerability; Harbour generational erosion. No KPI-card treatment.

slides.communicationGoal: Give the board the entire argument in one page without reproducing three mini-slides.
slides.headlineIntent: Pulse is strengthening, Northstar is vulnerable beneath the surface, and Harbour is weakening with future customers.
slides.hierarchy: One integrated competitive synopsis. Pulse/Northstar/Harbour are distinct narrative lanes, but not equal-sized dashboard cards.
slides.commentary: One sentence on what the combination means for competitive dynamics; no questionnaire recap.

slides.communicationGoal: Show who has competitive position today and who has momentum, so current size is not confused with direction of travel.
slides.headlineIntent: Northstar still owns the strongest position; Pulse owns the momentum.
slides.hierarchy: Pulse highlighted; Northstar contextual anchor; other brands muted but labelled directly.
annotations: Do not use five separate trend charts
slides.commentary: Explain that competitive position and momentum answer different questions.

slides.communicationGoal: Demonstrate the Pulse inflection over time and locate the campaign-period break without claiming causality.
slides.headlineIntent: Pulse has broken out of its old consideration range since Wave 3.
slides.hierarchy: One dominant Pulse series. Other brands appear only as faint context if useful; the Wave 3 inflection is annotated directly.
annotations: Do not display the inflated unweighted movement as a competing headline
slides.commentary: Pulse is now operating at a different consideration level than before Wave 3; this is observed tracker movement, not causal proof.

slides.communicationGoal: Show that Pulse's change is disproportionately concentrated among younger consumers.
slides.headlineIntent: Younger consumers are pulling Pulse forward faster than the market overall.
slides.hierarchy: Age gap is primary; campaign recognition is supporting context, not a second hero chart.
slides.commentary: The audience most responsive to the campaign period is also where consideration changes most strongly. Keep the relationship observational.

slides.communicationGoal: Show that Pulse perception and consideration have moved faster than customer conversion.
slides.headlineIntent: Pulse is becoming mentally available faster than it is becoming customers' provider.
slides.hierarchy: Use aligned W2/W5 stages or change markers. Emphasise the uneven conversion from awareness/image to usage rather than treating every stage equally.
slides.commentary: Synthesis is the value: upper-funnel and perception movement precede full behavioural conversion.

slides.communicationGoal: Make the contradiction between Northstar's external market strength and internal customer deterioration visually unavoidable.
slides.headlineIntent: Northstar still looks healthy from the outside. Its customers tell a different story.
slides.hierarchy: Two clearly separated universes: MARKET vs CURRENT CUSTOMERS. NPS collapse is dominant; stable awareness is the counterpoint.
annotations: Do not put awareness and NPS on one quantitative axis
slides.commentary: The risk is customer-led today; visibility has not yet absorbed the shock.

slides.communicationGoal: Assess whether Northstar's W5 recovery is broad enough to call the problem resolved.
slides.headlineIntent: Northstar is recovering in Wave 5, but the customer relationship has not simply reset.
slides.hierarchy: Four compact W3→W4→W5 recovery trajectories using consistent visual grammar. No dashboard chrome; label values directly.
slides.commentary: Distinguish partial recovery from evidence of a complete return to baseline.

slides.communicationGoal: Explain Harbour's strategic problem as a mismatch between today's installed base and tomorrow's acquisition audience.
slides.headlineIntent: Harbour's installed base is hiding an acquisition problem with younger consumers.
slides.hierarchy: Youth consideration trend is dominant. Current usage/installed-base evidence is contextual and should explain why total-market deterioration can look less dramatic.
slides.commentary: Harbour is not collapsing today; it is becoming harder to replenish tomorrow.

slides.communicationGoal: Close with the next management questions implied by the evidence rather than generic recommendations.
slides.headlineIntent: The next questions are about conversion, recovery and renewal.
slides.hierarchy: Three concise research/management questions, with no decorative KPI cards.
questions: Pulse — Can the brand convert younger-consumer consideration before campaign salience decays?
Northstar — Is Wave 5 recovery sufficient to protect loyalty, or is advocacy structurally impaired?
Harbour — Can the proposition recruit younger consumers before the existing customer base ages out?
slides.commentary: Implications should emerge from the prior argument. Do not introduce unsupported recommendations.

explicitlyRemoved.formerSlide: What we deliberately did not conclude
explicitlyRemoved.reason: Trustworthy editorial restraint should be visible in what the report chooses not to elevate. The report should not self-congratulate for ignoring low-base or inflated statistics. Methodological qualifications remain local only when they materially change interpretation.
